newsitem.title: CANADA: BCE shares rise on earnings momentum.
newsitem.headline: BCE shares rise on earnings momentum.

text.p: BCE Inc shares rose further on Monday, propelled by market expectations of strong earnings at the telecommunications company and its Northern Telecom Ltd unit, analysts said.

BCE rose 1.70 to 69.55 on more than 1.9 million shares in Toronto, just shy of its 52-week high of 69.75 and up from its year low of 47.25. BCE was up 1-3/8 to 51-3/4 in New York. Nortel fell 0.25 to 99.25 in Toronto and was unchanged at 73-5/8 in New York.
BCE's rise appeared to be driven mainly by retail investors, analysts said.
"It's retail buyers coming into what is a big retail stock anyway," said an analyst who declined to be identified.

The renewed interest in BCE, which has been building steadily over the last several months, was spurred last week when the company released strong year-end earnings. BCE posted a net profit of C$1.1 billion or C$3.40 a share in 1996, versus a 1995 profit of C$695 million or C$2.23 a share.
Although some analysts doubted how much further BCE shares could climb in the months ahead, John Drolet at Yorkton Securities Inc said he saw more upside to the stock.
"I think it has got a fair distance yet to go," Drolet said.

Drolet calculated BCE's net asset value at C$95 a share, compared with the mid-70s last year. One of the driving forces behind BCE's stock performance was the three-year restructuring program at its Bell Canada unit, which began in 1995 and was expected to cut C$1 billion from the telephone company's annual costs, Drolet said.
"That goes straight to BCE," he said.
Bell Canada has said it expected a 1997 profit of about C$950 million, compared with C$714 million in 1996.

Besides the company's earnings momentum, BCE's stock has been buoyed by its traditional role as an interest rate sensitive, dividend paying stock that benefited from Canada's declining interest rates over the past year.

Drolet said investors largely ignored BCE shares early in the stock market bull cycle, mainly because its Bell Canada unit was pummeled by competitors in the newly deregulated long-distance telephone market in Canada.
But with the restructuring at Bell Canada and new management since the company's long-distance monopoly, BCE was set to take on the competition, he said.
BCE's other operating subsidiaries and divisions were also poised for growth in 1997, Drolet said.
